:::writing{id="84327" variant="email" subject="Following Up on Support Conversation"}
Hi [Name],

I wanted to follow up after our last conversation. I’ll be honest, when I shared the details with my legal team and a few legally trained friends, it did not go over well. Their feedback was very clear that I was being far too accommodating given the circumstances and the legal reality in Tennessee.

As you know, we were married for seven years in the state of Tennessee. Under TN law, spousal support is based on the length of the marriage, the lifestyle that was established, and whether one spouse is economically disadvantaged after separation. I was advised that I clearly meet that standard, especially considering that you kept the home we were planning to live in and most of the furniture, while I am having to fully start over.

The amount we discussed previously simply will not work. It would not even come close to covering my medical expenses related to my neck issues, let alone rent, basic living expenses, or costs for D while he is still in high school. I have already submitted medical billing for review so deductibles and copays can be properly calculated, but even without that final number, it is clear the gap is significant.

Based on what has been reviewed, $3,500 per month for six months is the bare minimum needed for me to stabilize, secure appropriate housing, and not be forced into a situation that puts unnecessary hardship on me or D. This is not about excess. It is about having the ability to land on my feet after everything that has happened.

I would much prefer to work this out between us. If we cannot, I have been advised that the next step would be to let the court decide what is fair, at which point medical, financial, and therapy documentation would be turned over, along with consideration of attorney fees and debt allocation.

That is not my preference. I am still hoping we can handle this respectfully and without dragging things out. I appreciate you working with me to find a solution that reflects both the law and the reality of what it takes for me to start over.

Thank you for taking the time to consider this. I look forward to hearing back from you.

Bethany

Below is a **calm, legally grounded, and professional email** that preserves your leverage, references Tennessee law appropriately, and removes threats or inflammatory language while still making your position very clear. :::writing{id="73841" variant="email" subject="Request for Temporary Spousal Support Resolution"}
Hi [Name],

I want to start by saying that my sincere hope is still to resolve this matter respectfully and without unnecessary conflict. I appreciate your willingness to engage in conversation thus far, and I am hopeful we can reach a fair agreement that allows both of us to move forward.

After carefully reviewing the situation with legal counsel and legally trained advisors, I have been advised that the current proposal does not adequately reflect my legal rights under Tennessee law, given the length of our marriage and the standard of living established during that time.

As you know, we were married for seven years in the State of Tennessee. Under Tennessee statutes and case law, spousal support may be awarded when one spouse is economically disadvantaged relative to the other and requires assistance to maintain a standard of living reasonably comparable to that established during the marriage. This is particularly applicable where one spouse must incur significant costs to reestablish housing, furnishings, and stability following separation.

At the time of separation, you retained the marital residence we had planned to live in and removed the majority of the household furnishings. As a result, I am required to fully reestablish a household from the ground up while also managing ongoing living expenses, medical care related to my neck injury, and expenses for our child while he remains in high school.

Based on guidance from counsel and documentation currently being reviewed, the previously discussed amount would not come close to covering medical deductibles, copays, or baseline living expenses, let alone allow for reasonable stability during this transition period.

Accordingly, I am requesting temporary spousal support in the amount of $3,500 per month for a minimum period of six months following the finalization of the divorce. This request reflects the bare minimum necessary to secure appropriate housing, cover medical obligations, and avoid undue hardship during this legally recognized transition period. Additional medical billing is currently being reviewed to determine total out of pocket obligations.

My preference remains to resolve this privately and amicably. However, if we are unable to reach an agreement, I have been advised to proceed through formal legal channels, at which point medical, financial, and therapeutic documentation would be submitted for judicial determination, including consideration of attorney fees and associated costs.

I truly hope that will not be necessary. I believe honoring this request aligns with what you previously expressed, which was ensuring that we are stable and not placed in a position of unnecessary hardship. I remain open to resolving this in good faith and appreciate your cooperation in doing so.

Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to your response.

Sincerely,  
Bethany Gifford  
:::
